My side project died under its first real traffic spike. CPU pinned at 100%. My fix? Buy a bigger server. It worked... for two weeks. Then it died again.

Here's what scaling actually means, and the one idea that makes it work. 🧵

Scaling UP (vertical): give one machine more CPU/RAM.

✅ No code changes
❌ Hard ceiling (there's a biggest box)
❌ Gets expensive fast
❌ Single point of failure

A fine first move. A terrible long-term answer.

Scaling OUT (horizontal): run many machines behind a load balancer.

✅ No hard ceiling, just add nodes
✅ One dies, the rest serve
✅ Cheap commodity boxes

The catch: your app has to be DESIGNED for it. That's where people get stuck.

The thing that makes scaling out work: STATELESS services.

If a user's session lives in one server's memory, their next request hits another server... and they're logged out.

Any server must be able to handle any request.

"Stateless" doesn't mean no state. It means state moves OUT of your app servers:

• Sessions → shared cache (Redis)
• Durable data → database
• Files → object storage (S3)

Now your servers are cattle, not pets. Kill them, add more, no ceremony.

The mindset shift: stop asking "how big a machine do I need?" and start asking "what breaks if I run 10 copies of this?"

Full post (first in my System Design series):
https://blog.sandeepallala.com/blog/system-design-scalability-scaling-up-vs-out
